comments.author: @mrnobody3161
comments.text:
4,000 to an estamated 50,000 abandoned wells in Onterrible.
120,000+ abandoned wells is a "conservative" estimate in Oilberduh. 
I also wonder about all the holes in the ground and the long term affects of rain and the erosion going on we don't know about.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That’s the part that really stuck with me too. The wells themselves may be forgotten, but the long-term effects don’t necessarily disappear with them. Groundwater movement, erosion, deteriorating well casings and possible leakage can all become problems decades later. And when nobody even knows exactly how many old wells are out there, monitoring them becomes a huge challenge. Thanks for adding that perspective.

replies.text: Canada certainly has plenty of oil resources, but extraction comes down to more than policy alone. Ontario actually still has over 3,000 active oil and gas wells. The fascinating part is how much of that original 1858 boom is still affecting the province today.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Exactly. Those Ontario ‘Hard Oilers’ became highly sought-after drillers and carried their techniques into the U.S. and eventually oil fields all over the world. That’s one of the wildest parts of this story, southwestern Ontario ended up exporting oil expertise far beyond Canada.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: The video isn’t referring to American money. The Province of Canada officially adopted dollars and cents in the 1850s, and by 1858 Canadian accounts were being kept in dollars. So using ‘dollars’ for that period is historically correct.

comments.author: @maryjeanjones7569
comments.text: The first oil discovery in Canada was in 1858 in Southern Ontario.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Exactly, Oil Springs, Ontario, is where James Miller Williams established Canada’s first commercial oil well in 1858. Oil had been known in the region before that, but 1858 is the key date for the start of commercial production.
